       for supported provers. By default, Alt-Ergo is selected, but you may specify another decision
       procedure or a list of to try with. Finally, you should supply none for this option to skip the
       proof step.
       It is possible to ask for several decision procedures to be tried. For each goal, the first decision
       procedure that succeeds cancels the other attempts.
       You may also select provers "tip" to use proof strategies and "script" to use proof scripts
       (without applying new proof strategies), see option "-wp-script" below for more details.

-wp-script <mode> selects how to manage proof strategies and proof scripts session. Several modes
       are available:

           - "batch" use existing scripts, but do not store new scripts. This is the default mode for
              prover "script".

           - "update" use existing scripts and store new or updated scripts in proof session. This is the
              default mode for prover tip.

           - "init" don't use existing scripts and store the newly generated scripts in proof session.
           - "dry" don't use existing script and don't store any new scripts in proof session.

       This parameter can be customized using the FRAMAC_WP_SCRIPT environment variable. If both
       the variable and the option are positioned, the option has the priority.

-wp-interactive <mode> selects the interaction mode with interactive provers such as Coq (while
       it could work for other interactive provers, it has not been tested so far). Five modes are available:

           - "batch" mode only check existing scripts (the default);
           - "update" mode update the script and then checks it;
           - "edit" mode opens the default prover editor on each generated goal;
           - "fix" mode only opens editor for non-proved goals;
           - "fixup" combines "update" and "fix" (if necessary).

       New scripts are created in the interactive directory of WP session (see option -wp-session
       <dir>).

-wp-list-provers lists all available provers. The option prints all the available provers from Why3
       configuration and from the current PATH with their respective version and -wp-prover <p>
       code name. See -wp-why3-config and -wp-why3-detect for details.

<!-- page 40 -->

-wp-(no)-run-all-provers Run all specified provers on each goal not proved by Qed. When a
       prover succeeds in proving the goal, the others are not stopped. (default is: no).

-wp-strategy s,... specifies the default ones to be used, see Section 2.5 for details.

-wp-gen only generates proof obligations, does not run provers. See option -wp-out to obtain the
       generated proof obligations.

-wp-par <n> limits the number of parallel process runs for decision procedures. Default is the number
       of logical cores on the machine. With -wp-par 1, the order of logged results is fixed. With more
       processes, the order is runtime dependent.

-wp-filename-truncation <n> truncates the basename of proof obligation files to the first n
       characters. Since numbers can be added as suffixes to ensure unique filenames, their length can be
       longer than n. No truncation is performed when the value equals zero. (default is: 60)

-wp-(no)-proof-trace asks for provers to output extra information on proved goals when available
       (default is: no).

-wp-timeout <t> sets the timeout (in seconds) for the calls to the decision prover (defaults to 2
       seconds).

-wp-memlimit <m> sets the memory-limit (in Mb) for the calls to the decision prover (defaults to
       1000 Mb).

-wp-fct-timeout <f1:t1,f2:t2,...> customize the timeout for each specified function (t1 for
       f1, t2 for f2, etc).

-wp-interactive-timeout <n> sets the timeout (in seconds) for checking edited scripts with
       interactive provers (defaults to 30 seconds).

-wp-(no)-script-on-stdout displays generated proof scripts on stdout instead of saving them on
       disk (default is: no).

-wp-time-extra <n> additional time allocated to provers when replaying a script. This is used to
       cope with variable machine load. Default is 5s.

-wp-time-margin <n> margin time for considering a proof to be replayable without a script. When
       a proof succeed within timeout-margin seconds, it is considered fully automatic. Otherwise, a
       script is created by prover tip to register the proof time. This is used to decrease the impact of
       machine load when proof time is closed to the timeout. Default is 5s.

-wp-steps <n> sets the maximal number of prover steps. This can be used as a machine-independent
       alternative to timeout.

-wp-why3-config=<file> use the specified Why3 configuration file for configuring provers. By
       default, uses '$HOME/.why3.conf' if it exists.

-wp-(no)-why3-detect collect all available provers from $PATH in addition to the specified or
       default Why3 configuration (set by default).

-wp-why3-opt='options,...' provides additional options to the why3 command.

-wp-why3-extra-config='files,...' provides additional configuration files for why3.

-wp-prepare-scripts initialize a script tracking directory in the session directory.

-wp-finalize-scripts remove untracked scripts according to the tracking directory if it does exist
       (does not remove anything otherwise).

-wp-dry-finalize-scripts scripts that might be removed by -wp-finalize-scripts are kept,
       a message is printed instead for each file. The marks directory is kept.

<!-- page 41 -->

Example of using provers. Suppose you have the following configuration:

      # frama-c -wp-list-provers
      [wp] Prover Alt-Ergo 2.0.0 [alt-ergo|altergo|Alt-Ergo:2.0.0]
      [wp] Prover CVC4 1.6 [cvc4|CVC4:1.6]
      [wp] Prover CVC4 1.6 [cvc4-ce|CVC4:1.6,counterexamples]
      [wp] Prover Eprover 2.4 [eprover|Eprover:2.4]
      [wp] Prover Z3 4.8.7 [z3-ce|Z3:4.8.7:counterexamples]

     Then, to use (for instance) CVC4 1.6, you can use -wp-prover cvc4 or -wp-prover CVC4:1.6.
Similarly, if you want to use Z3 4.6.0 without bitvectors, you can use -wp-prover z3-nobv. Finally,
since Why-3 also provides the alias altergo for this prover, -wp-prover altergo will also run it
via Why-3.

     If you require on command line a specific version of a prover which is not installed, WP will emit an
error. When a script contains a couple prover/version that is not installed, WP will try to find another
version of the same prover and fallback on this solver (emitting a warning) if it finds one. In this case,
one should update the scripts.

     Notice that Why-3 provers benefit from a cache management when used in combination with a
WP-session, see Section 2.4.14 for more details.

#### 2.4.9 Generated Proof Obligations

Your proof obligations are generated and saved to several text files. With the -wp-out option, you can
specify a directory of your own where all these files are generated. By default, this output directory
is determined as follows: in the GUI, it is <home>/.frama-c-wp where <home> is the user's home
directory returned by the HOME environment variable. In command-line, a temporary directory is
automatically created and removed when Frama-C exits.

     Other options controlling the output of generated proof obligations are:

-wp-print pretty-prints the generated proof obligations on the standard output. Results obtained by
        provers are reported as well.

-wp-status pretty-prints only proof obligations that are not (yet) proved on the standard output. In
        case of script, prints all the non-proved sub-goals of the script.

-wp-out <dir> sets the user directory where proof obligations are saved. The directory is created if
        it does not exist yet. Its content is not cleaned up automatically.

#### 2.4.10 Probes and Counter Examples

Introduced since Frama-C 29.0 (Copper)
     Depending on prover capabilities, WP can trigger counter example generation for non successful

goals. Provers supporting counter example generation can be identified by the "counterexamples"
variant after their name. For example, in the prover selection example above, cvc4-ce and z3-ce are
such provers.

     To enable counter examples generation by WP you shall use -wp-counter-examples option.
Then, for each selected solver that has a counter-examples variant, this variant will be used instead
and counter-examples will be asked to the solver in case of unknown result. Notice that you can
also use counter-examples solvers without asking for counter-examples. For instance, with option
-wp-prover cvc4-ce, WP will use this version of the prover, even if counter examples is not active;
the prover will not be asked to report models, unless counter examples is activate. Notice that solvers
variants with counter-examples support are generally a bit slower than their original version.

     A proof obligation for which a counter-example has been generated is reported by WP by the string
"(Model)" after its proof status. For instance:

<!-- page 42 -->

 # ./bin/frama-c -wp ~/work/wrong.i -wp-prover cvc4 -wp-counter-examples

[...]

[wp] 6 goals scheduled

[wp] [Unknown] typed_g_ensures (Qed 4ms) (CVC4) (No Cache) (Model)

[wp] [Cache] not used

[wp] Proved goals: 6 / 7

Unreachable: 1

Qed:      5 (0.72ms)

Unknown:  1

     Notice that cache usage is disabled for provers asked to generate a counter-example, since models are
currently not stored in WP's cache5.

     A counter-example consists in a Model, that is, a map from Variables or Probes (see below) to Values,
for which the proof obligation formula is expected to be False. More precisely, the Model reports
on necessary conditions for the proof obligation to be wrong, although they might not be sufficient in
practice.

     Generated models are reported by WP along with prover results when either -wp-print or
-wp-status options are used. The interactive proof transformer (TIP) also displays models in the
graphical user interface, when available.

     Probes are generalization of variables. They are named expressions for which the prover is asked to
output a value in the model. WP will automatically introduce probes for formal parameters of functions
and universally quantified variables of lemmas. Developers can introduce their own probes by using the
@probe annotation. For instance:

   int a[4][5];
   /*@

       ensures \false;
       assigns \nothing;
   */
   int value(int i, int j) {
       //@ probe Offset: &a[i][j] - &a[0][0];
       return a[i][j];
   }
}

    Probes must be named ACSL terms. As a short cut, for very simple probes such as variables, the
name can be omitted. Several probes might have the same name, although it is not really convenient for
debugging. The general syntax for the annotation is:

                          probe a1 : t1, . . . , an : tn ;

    Probes are normalized by Qed during simplification of proof obligations by WP. Their (simplified)
term definitions are reported when printing proof obligations, and their model values are reported when
printing proof results, when available. For instance:

        # frama-c [...] -wp-status
        [...]
        Goal Post-condition (file /Users/correnson/work/matrix.i, line 3) in 'value':
        Assume {

          Type: is_sint32(i) /\ is_sint32(j).
          Probe i = i.
          Probe j = j.
          Probe Offset = ((4 * j) + (20 * i)) / 4.
        }

5 This feature might be added in future versions of the plugin.

<!-- page 43 -->

Prove: false.            Unknown  (Model)  (Qed:2ms)
Prover CVC4 1.8 returns
Model i = 0
Model j = 0
Model Offset = 0
[...]

    User probes are always reported, even if -wp-counter-examples is not activated. This feature
reveals to be extremely useful for debugging proofs in practice, even when counter examples is not
available or not activated. It also helps in understanding C, ACSL and WP models and encoding.

    You may freely add as many probes as you want: probes do not modify the proof obligations
submitted to the provers, unless -wp-counter-examples is activated. For instance, in the previous
example:

 # frama-c [...] -wp-status -wp-no-counter-examples
[...]
Goal Post-condition (file /Users/correnson/work/matrix.i, line 3) in 'value':
Assume {

  Type: is_sint32(i) /\ is_sint32(j).
  Probe Offset = ((4 * j) + (20 * i)) / 4.
}
Prove: false.
Prover CVC4 1.8 returns Unknown (Qed:2ms) (Cached)
[...]

Summary of WP options related to probes and counter-examples generation:

-wp-(no)-counter-examples enables counter examples generation for supporting provers. Also
       generate probes for formal parameters of functions and universal quantifiers of lemmas. Not set by
       default.

-wp-print, -wp-status pretty-prints the probes and the associated models, when available.

-wp-solver xxx-ce use the specified variant of prover, even when counter-examples is not activated.

-wp-(no)-probes registers the @probe ACSL extension in Frama-C kernel. This option is set by
       default, but you may want to deactivate it to avoid any clash with extensions from other plugins.

#### 2.4.11 Additional Proof Libraries

It is possible to add additional bases of knowledge to decision procedures thanks to the following option:

-wp-share <dir> modifies the default directory where resources are found. This option can be useful
       for running a modified or patched distribution of WP.

#### 2.4.12 Linking ACSL Symbols to External Libraries

DEPRECATED. You shall now import a Why3 module instead of using custom drivers. See
Section 2.4.13 for details.

    Besides additional proof libraries, it is also possible to link declared ACSL symbols to external or
predefined symbols. In such case, the corresponding ACSL definitions, if any, are not exported by WPs.

    External linkage is specified in driver files. It is possible to load one or several drivers with the
following WP plug-in option:

-wp-driver <file,...> load specified driver files.

    Each driver file contains a list of bindings with the following syntax:

<!-- page 44 -->

library "lib": "lib" . . . "lib"

  group.field  := string                         = "link" ;
  group.field  += string                         = "link" ;
               symbol                            = property-tags "link" ;
         type  type symbol ( type,. . . ,type )  = "link" ;
         ctor  type symbol ( type,. . . ,type )
       logic   symbol ( type,. . . ,type )
predicate

    It is also possible to define aliases to other ACSL symbols, rather than external links. In this case,
you may replace = by := and use an ACSL identifier in place of the external "link". No property tag is
allowed when defining aliases.

    Library specification is optional and applies to subsequent linked symbols. If provided, the WP
plug-in automatically loads the specified external libraries when linked symbols are used in a goal.
Dependencies among libraries can also be specified, after the ':'.

    Generic group.field options have a specific value for each theory. The binding applies to the current
theory. Binding with the := operator resets the option to the singleton of the given string and binding
with the += operator adds the given string to the current value of the option. The following options are
defined by the plugin: why3.file and why3.import.

    C-Comments are allowed in the file. For overloaded ACSL symbols, it is necessary to provide one
"link" symbol for each existing signature. The same "link" symbol is used for all provers, and must be
defined in the specified libraries, or in the external ones (see 2.4.11).

    Alternatively, a link-name can be an arbitrary string with patterns substituted by arguments,
"(%1+%2)" for instance.

    When a library "lib" is specified, the loaded module depends on the option:

               Option             Format
               why3.file          path.why[:name][:as]
               why3.import        theory[:as]

    Precise meaning of formats is given by the following examples (all filenames are relatives to the driver
file's directory):

why3.file="mydir/foo.why" Imports theory foo.Foo from directory mydir.

why3.file="mydir/foo.why:Bar" Imports theory foo.Bar from directory mydir.

why3.file="mydir/foo.why:Bar:T" Imports theory foo.Bar as T from directory mydir.

why3.import="foo.Bar" Imports theory foo.Bar with no additional includes.

why3.import="foo.Bar:T" Imports theory foo.Bar as T with no additional includes.

    See also the default WP driver file, in [wp-share]/wp.driver.
    Optional property-tags can be given to logic "link" symbols to allow the WP plugin to perform
additional simplifications (See section 4). Tags consist of an identifier with column (':'), sometimes
followed by a link ('"link";'). The available tags are depicted on figure 2.5.

<!-- page 45 -->

   Tags               Operator Properties
commutative:          specify a commutative symbol: x ⊙ y = y ⊙ x
associative:          specify an associative symbol: (x ⊙ y) ⊙ z = x ⊙ (y ⊙ z)
ac:                   shortcut for associative: commutative:
left:                 balance the operator on left during export to solvers (requires the
right:                associative tag): x ⊙ y ⊙ z = (x ⊙ y) ⊙ z
absorbent: "a-link":  balance the operator on right during export to solvers (requires
                      the associative tag): x ⊙ y ⊙ z = x ⊙ (y ⊙ z)
neutral: "e-link":    specify "a-link" as being the absorbent element of the symbol:
                      "a-link" ⊙ x = "a-link"
invertible:           x ⊙ "a-link" = "a-link"
                      specify "e-link" as being the neutral element of the symbol:
idempotent:           "e-link" ⊙ x = x
injective:            x ⊙ "e-link" = x
constructor:          specify simplification relying on the existence of an inverse:
                      x ⊙ y = x ⊙ z ⇐⇒ y = z
                      y ⊙ x = z ⊙ x ⇐⇒ y = z
                      specify an idempotent symbol: x ⊙ x = x
                      specify an injective function:
                      f (x1, . . . , xn) = f (y1, . . . , yn) =⇒ ∀i xi = yi
                      specify an injective function, that constructs different values from
                      any other constructor. Formally, whenever f and g are two dis-
                      tinct constructors, they are both injective and: f (x1, . . . , xn)̸ =
                      g(y1, . . . , ym) forall xi and yj.

                      Figure 2.5: Driver Property Tags

<!-- page 46 -->

#### 2.4.13 Importing Why3 Modules

The WP plug-in provides an ACSL module importer that can import Why3 theories and modules into
ACSL. See Frama-C user manual, Section § 6.3 for details. Here is an example of use:

     //@ import \wp::why3: number::Gcd;
     /*@

         assigns \nothing;
         ensures \result == Gcd::gcd(a,b);
     */
     int euclid(int a, int b)
     {
         int r;
         /*@

            loop assigns a, b, r;
            loop invariant Gcd::gcd(a,b) == \at( Gcd::gcd(a,b), Pre );
            loop variant \abs(b);
         */
         while( b != 0 ) {
            r=b;
            b=a%b;
            a=r;
         }
         return a < 0 ? -a : a;
     }
The Why3 load-path can be specified from the command-line:
-wp-library <dir,...> add the specified directory to the Why3 load-path.
Notice that the Why3 standard library is already in the load-path by default.

<!-- page 47 -->

#### 2.4.14 Proof Session & Cache

The WP plugin can use a session directory to store information to be used from one execution to another
one. It is used to store proof scripts edited from the TIP (see Section 2.3) and to replay them from the
command line. And it is also used to speedup the invocation of provers by reusing previous runs.

    Actually, running provers can be demanding in terms of memory and CPU resources. When working
interactively or incrementally, it is often the case where most proof obligations remain unchanged from
one WP execution to the other. To reduce this costs, a cache of prover results can be used and stored in
your session.

    There are different ways of using the cache, depending on your precise needs. The main option to
control cache usage is -wp-cache, documented below:

-wp-cache <mode> selects the cache mode to use with Why-3 provers. The default mode is update if
       there is WP session available, and none otherwise. The environment variable FRAMAC_WP_CACHE
       can be used for the same purpose, if both the environment variable and the option are configured,
       the option is prioritary.

-wp-cache-dir <dir> select the directory where cached results are stored. By default, the cache is
       store in the WP session directory. The environment variable FRAMAC_WP_CACHEDIR can be used
       to customize the directory, if both the environment variable and the option are configured, the
       option is prioritary.

    The available cache modes are described below:

-wp-cache update : use cache entries or run the provers, and store new results in the cache. This
       mode is useful when you are working interactively : proofs can be partial and volatile, and you
       want to accumulate and keep as much previous results as you can.

-wp-cache cleanup : same as update mode but at the end of Frama-C execution, any cache entry
       that was not used nor updated will be deleted. This mode shall be only used when you want to
       cleanup your cache with old useless entries, typically at the end of an interactive session.

-wp-cache replay : same as update mode but new results are not stored in the cache. This mode
       is useful for continuous integration, when you are not sure your cache is complete but don't want
       to modify it.

-wp-cache offline : similar to replay mode but cache entries are the unique source of results.
       Provers are never run and missing cache entries would result in a « Failed » verdict. This mode is
       useful to fasten continuous integration and enforcing cache completeness.

-wp-cache rebuild : force prover execution and store all results in the cache. Previous results will
       be replaced with new ones, but entries for non relevant proofs would be kept and you might need
       a cleanup stage after. This mode is useful when you modify your Why-3 or prover installation and
       you don't want to reuse your previous cache entries.

-wp-cache none : do not use nor modify cache entries; provers are run normally. This option
       must be used if you have a session set and you don't want to use the cache, since the default is
       mode update in this case. But you probably always to benefit from a cache when you have an
       (interactive) session.

    When using cache with a non-offline mode, time and steps limits recorded in the cache are
compared to the command line settings to produce meaningful and consistent results. Hence, if you
provide more time or more steps from the command line than before, the prover would be run again. If
you provide less or equal limits, the cache entries are reused, but WP still report the cached time and
step limits to inform you of your previous attempts. For instance, if you have in the cache a « Valid »
entry with time 12.4s and re-run it with a timeout of 5s, you will have a « Timeout » result with time
12.4s printed on the console.

<!-- page 48 -->

#### 2.4.15 Proof Obligation Reports

The WP plug-in can export statistics on generated proof obligations. These statistics are called WP
reports and are distinct from those property reports generated by the Report plug-in. Actually, WP
reports are statistics on proof obligations generated by WP, whereas property reports are consolidated
status of properties, generated by the Frama-C kernel from various analyzers. We only discuss WP
reports in this section.

    Reports are generated with the following command-line options:

-wp-report <Rspec1,...,Rspecn> specifies the list of reports to export. Each value Rspeci is a
       report template specification file. See Section 2.8 for details on their structure.

-wp-report-basename <name> set the basename for exported reports (described below).

-wp-report-json <file>.json output the proof report in JSON format. See Section 2.7 for
       details on the JSON report format.

#### 2.4.16 Persistent Options

As a general observation, almost none of the internal WP data is kept in memory after each execution.
Most of the generated proof-obligation data is stored on disk before being sent to provers, and they are
stored in a temporary directory that is removed upon Frama-C exit (see also -wp-out option).

    The only information which is added to the Frama-C kernel consists in a new status for those
properties proved by WP plug-in with their dependencies.

    Thus, when combining WP options with -then, -save and -load options, the user should be
aware of the following precisions:

-wp, -wp-prop, -wp-fct, -wp-bhv. These options make the WP plug-in generate proof-
       obligations for the selected properties. The values of these options are never saved and they
       are cleared by -then. Hence, running -wp-prop A -then -wp-fct F does what you expect:
       properties tagged by A are proved only once.

-wp-print, -wp-status, -wp-prover, -wp-gen, -wp-detect. These options do not gen-
       erate new proof-obligations, but run other actions on all previously generated ones. For the same
       reasons, they are not saved and cleared by -then.

-wp-xxx. All other options are tunings that can be easily turned on and off or set to the desired value.
       They are saved and kept across -then commands.

### 2.5 Proof Strategies

Introduced since Frama-C 28.0 (Nickel)
    Proof obligations generated by WP are usually discharged by an SMT solver specified by the user

through command line option -wp-prover. As described in previous sections, complex proof obligations
may also be split into simpler sub-goals by applying Tactics from the TIP user interface.

    Proof strategies provide user-defined heuristics to automatically try various combinations of provers,
timeouts and tactics, depending on the proof context. This is a much more effective technique than
relying on manually edited scripts through the TIP user interface. Here are some benefits of using proof
strategies:

    - Proof strategies are automatic: there is no need for entering GUI session.
    - Proof strategies can be associated to individual functions, lemmas or properties, or tried globally.
    - Tactics are applied following patterns: depending on your case study, you can define fine-tuned

       strategies to solve your common issues.

<!-- page 49 -->

     - Proof strategies are compatible with TIP-based scripts: you can use strategies to complete scripts
        and conversely.

     - Scripts are easier to replay and to update: each proof node now records which strategy was involved
        in the past, so that incomplete or broken proofs can be recovered easily.

     To activate proof strategies and search for new scripts for unproven goals, user shall activate the tip
prover from the command line, with -wp-prover tip, or use the interfactive TIP from the graphical
user interface.

     Proof Strategies are defined thanks to dedicated ACSL extensions and controlled by specific
command-line options. Note that those extensions are only available unless command-line option
-wp-no-strategy-engine is specified. The syntax of ACSL extensions for proof strategies is defined
below:

                                         @\wp::strategy name :
                                               alternative ,
                                               ...,
                                               alternative ;

                                         @\wp::proof name : target , . . . , target ;

     A strategy must be defined by a unique name and consists of a list of alternatives that will be tried
in order until proof completion.

     Proof hints can be specified to associate strategies to lemma, function or property names. Hints
consists of a strategy name to be used for one or many proof targets. Targets follow the same conventions
than -wp-prop command-line option, although quotes might be necessary, e.g. "@requires". A
proof hint specification applies for all properties matching the property filter. Many proof hints might
apply, in which case, proof hints will be tried in order.

     Strategies shall be defined before being used as proof hints. It is recommended to write strategies in
separated *.c or *.i files and to write proof hints right after their target definition.

     Strategy consists of list of alternatives with the following syntax:

                                         alternative ::=
                                            | \prover("p" , . . . , "p", timeout)
                                            | \tactic("id", param , . . . , param)
                                            | \auto("id" , . . . , "id")
                                            | \default
                                            | strategy

     Each form alternative consists of one possible solution to discharge a proof obligation:

     - \provers(p,...,p,time) will try the specified provers in sequence with a specified timeout.
        Provers and/or timeout can be omitted, in such a case the command-line options -wp-prover
        and -wp-timeout are used instead. Sub-second timeout can also be specified, eg. 0.2 for 200
        milliseconds. Prover names must be individually quoted, with the same syntax as -wp-prover
        command line option.

     - \tactic(id,prm...) will try to apply the specified tactic with the associated parameters.
        Tactic parameters allow to select the target of the tactic, and the strategy to be used on generated
        sub-goals.

     - \auto(id,...) will try to apply the (deprecated) auto-strategies available in WP versions prior
        to Cobalt.

     - name or \default tries the specified strategy.

     The default strategy consists in applying the strategies specified through the command-line option
-wp-strategy s,..., in order.

     Tactic parameters are specified using the following syntax:

<!-- page 50 -->

                                               param ::=
                                                  | \goal(pattern,. . . )
                                                  | \when(pattern,. . . )
                                                  | \ingoal(pattern,. . . )
                                                  | \incontext(pattern,. . . )
                                                  | \pattern(pattern,. . . )
                                                  | \select(value)
                                                  | \param(id,value)
                                                  | \child(id,strategy)
                                                  | \children(strategy)

    Tactic parameters are interpreted as follows:

    - \goal(ps), \when(ps) and other patterns are used to match parts of the current proof node.
       The form \when(ps) looks for top-level hypotheses patterns, \goal(ps) for top-level goal
       patterns. Form \ingoal(ps) and \incontext(ps) respectectively matches patterns deeper
       inside the goal or the hypotheses, and finally \pattern(ps) searches in the entire proof obligation.
       When several patterns are given, all must apply and agree on common pattern variables. Pattern
       syntax is specified below.

    - \select(v) defines the main target of the selected tactic. The value v uses the same syntax as
       patterns, with pattern variables replaced with their matched values. Few tactics support multiple
       selection, in which case, multiple values can be provided. When no selection is specified, the first
       specified pattern is used as an implicit target. When no selection nor pattern is selected, the
       default selection is the proof goal.

    - \param(p,v) configures the parameter value p of the selected tactic with the associated value.
    - \child(a,s) applies strategy s to prove the sub-goal named a of the tactic.
    - \children(s) applies strategy s on (other) sub-goals of the tactic. If unspecified, the strategy

       used for the current node is applied.

    Tactics identifiers and their parameters can be obtained from the command line:

    - frama-c -wp-tactic ? lists all the registered tactic identifiers;
    - frama-c -wp-tactic id,... prints detailed infos for the selected tactics.

    Patterns and values are a closed to raw proof obligation formulae, with the following restrictions and
meaning:

    - variables are pattern variables;
    - pattern _ matches any value;
    - pattern x:p matches pattern p and bind its value to variable x;
    - pattern a..b matches integer constants in the specified (constant) range.
    - pattern \any(p,...) matches any of the specified patterns.
    - patterns p[k] and p[k->v] matches array operations, e.g. for memory models;
    - ACSL operators have their usual meaning;
    - ACSL list operators [|...|], ^ and *^ are also recognized;
    - function calls must use their printed name, as they appear in proof nodes;
    - for function patterns, trailing dots can be used to match any number of arguments, like in

       f(x,y,(..)) for instance.

    It is highly recommended using the graphical user interface or -wp-print to build patterns expression
and values.

Smoking Strategies. When smoke-tests are activated by -wp-smoke-tests, strategies are deacti-
vated by default on smoking goals. Indeed, smoke tests are proof obligations that are expected to fail.
However, it might be interesting to try strategies on smoking proof goals in order to stress-test further
your code. To activate strategies for smoke-tests, you shall add the smoke name to the strategies to use:

<!-- page 51 -->

@\wp::proof strategy : smoke,target , . . . , target ;

### 2.6 Structure of JSON Scripts

The proof scripts generated by using the Interactive Proof Editor (Section 2.3) are saved in the
Frama-C/WP session as JSON files. This section defines the format of session scripts precisely.

    JSON scripts files are located in the <session>/wp/scripts sub-directory of the Frama-C session
directory (set with command line option -session) or in the <wpsession>/scripts sub-directory
of the Frama-C/WP session directory (set with command line option -wp-session).

    The proof scripts for goal named <goal> is stored in a single file <goal>.json ; the format of the
<goal> name is identical to the one used by the Frama-C/Report plug-in for its JSON output.

    The content of each script file is an array of alternatives, each alternative being a record with two
possible structures, that might represent a prover attempt or the application of a tactic:

                 wp.script ::= [wp.alternative, . . . ]
           wp.alternative ::= wp.prover | wp.tactic

Prover Attempts The proof script records previous attempts to discharge a proof obligation with
external provers (also called decision procedures). Each attempt is represented by a JSON record with
the following fields:

wp.prover           "prover" :                   
                 "verdict" :    string,
                                 wp.verdict, 
           ::=          "time" :   number ?
                    "steps" :   number? 
                     "depth" :   number ?

wp.verdict ::= "none" | "valid" | "unknown" |
                    "timeout" | "stepout" | "invalid" | "failed"

    Remark that, since the proof scripts do not record the proof obligation that was exercised, there
is no guarantee that replaying the script on a (potentially new) proof obligation would issue the same
result. Hence, prover attempts must not be used as a cache, but can serve as a hint for choosing among
several alternatives.

Proof Tactic Applying a tactic is represented by a JSON record with the following fields:

                                                        
                    "tactic" :     string,
                    "header" :     string? 
                      "select" :     wp.selection,
wp.tactic  ::=         "params" :
                 "children" :      { string : wp.param, . . . }?
                 "strategy" :      { string : wp.script, . . . }? 
                                     string?

    The header field is just a descriptive title and has no special meaning. The tactic identifies
the tactic, as it has been registered in the Frama-C/WP internal API. The selection is an opaque
encoding of the target of the tactic inside the proof obligation structure. The params array stores the
value of tactic parameters, if any. The children stores the proof scripts associated with each sub-goal
generated by applying the specified tactic on a proof obligation. Finally, the strategy fields is used to
recall which user-defined proof strategy was used to trigger the tactic (See Section 2.5).

<!-- page 52 -->

Tactic Parameters Values of tactical parameters are encoded with the following JSON format,
depending on the internal type of the parameter value:

wp.param ::= bool | number | string

| wp.named | wp.selection                        
                                      string, 
                     "id" :           string? 
                                       string?
wp.named ::=null |   "title" :

                      "description" :

    Named items (wp.named) corresponds, for instance, to searched lemmas. Selections corresponds to
terms or expressions selected by the user via the graphical user interface, like the target of the tactic, as
described below.

Tactic Selection The target of the tactic is identified by a complex structure encoding on which part
of the proof obligation it shall be applied. Since the exact structure of the proof obligation may vary
from time to time, this structure allows for searching in the proof obligation a pattern that resembles the
original target that was originally selected by the user during an interactive session with the Frama-C/WP
graphical user interface.

    Such patterns are encoded as follows:

wp.selection ::= null
                   | { "select" : "clause goal", wp.pattern }
                   | { "select" : "inside goal", wp.occur, wp.pattern }
                   | { "select" : "clause step", wp.at, wp.kind, wp.pattern }
                   | { "select" : "inside step", wp.at, wp.kind, wp.occur, wp.pattern }
                   | { "select" : "range", "min" : number, "max" : number }
                   | { "select" : "kint", "val" : number }
                   | { "select" : "compose", "id" : string, "args" : [wp.selection, . . .] }

 wp.pattern ::= "pattern" : string
    wp.occur ::= "occur" : number
        wp.at ::= "at" : number
     wp.kind ::= "kind" : "have"|"type"|"init"|"branch"|"either"|"state"

    The various components of selection patterns have the following meaning: wp.pattern encodes a
term or predicate pattern; wp.occur designates which occurrence of the pattern to select, in case of
there is many of them inside the selected goal or hypothesis; wp.at designates the order of the selected
hypothesis inside the proof obligation (the pattern is searched around this value), and wp.kind its kind.

    The wp.pattern is a simple string that encodes the head of the structure of the selected term or
formulæ inside the designated goal or hypothesis. It is the concatenation of the first 32 head nodes of
width-first traversal of the selected term, each node being represented by the following string:

    - constant are represented by their value,
    - free variables by their base-name prefixed with $,
    - bound variables by their de-Bruijn index prefixed with #,
    - true and false by T and F, and quantifiers by \F and \E,
    - operators by &,|,!,~,+,-,*,/,%<,>,=,>=,/,?
    - array operations by [], [.] and [=]

<!-- page 53 -->

    - record operations by .fd and {fd,...}
    - function calls by their name
    For instance, the term (x1 ≤ x2 + 1) will be represented by the pattern "<=$x+$x1".

Script Priority When several alternatives are available for discharging a proof obligation, the script
and tip provers of Frama-C/WP choose which one to apply first according to the following heuristic:

   1. try internal prover "Qed" with a "valid" verdict;
   2. try any SMT prover with a "valid" verdict;
   3. try the "Coq" proof assistant with a "valid" verdict;
   4. try any Tactic alternative;
   5. finally try the remaining Prover alternatives.
    Inside the same level of priority, alternatives are kept in their original order.

### 2.7 Structure of JSON Reports

The generated JSON report format consists of an array of JSON records, one for each generated toplevel
goal. Each record consists of the following fields, some of them being optional when indicated:

"goal":<string> goal identifier (same as in console report);
"property":<string> property identifier (see Frama-C/Report documentation);
"file":<string> source file location;
"line":<number> source line location;
"axiomatic"?:<string> axiomatic name (optional);
"function"?:<string> function name (optional);
"behavior"?:<string> behavior name (optional, non-default);
"smoke":<boolean> smoke-tests goal (warning: Cf. fields "verdict" and "passed" below);
"verdict":<string> prover returned status. Can be "none", "valid", "failed",

       "unknown", "stepout" or "timeout" (warning: Cf. field "passed" below);
"passed":<boolean> is "true" when the prover verdict is valid for non-smoke tests, or when the

       prover verdict is not valid for smoke tests;
"script"?:<string> script file, when available (optional);
"tactics"?:<number> number of tactics involved in the script (optional);
"provers":[<prover>,...] prover detailed output. Each entry of the array is a record that

       consists of the following fields:

       "prover":<string> prover name (with version, see option -wp-prover);
       "time":<number> prover time, in milliseconds. For Qed prover, includes also the total

              simplification time for other provers and tactics that contributes to the goal;
       "success":<number> number of valid sub-goals the prover contributes to.

"subgoals"?:<number> number of associated sub-goals (optional, when more than one);
"proved"?:<number> number of sub-goals proved (optional, when non-zero);
"failed"?:<number> number of sub-goals ending with prover failure or failed smoke-tests (optional,

       when non-zero);

<!-- page 54 -->

"timeout"?:<number> number of sub-goals ending in timeout or step-out (except for smoke-tests)
       (optional, when non-zero);

"unknown"?:<number> number of sub-goals with unknown verdict (except for smoke-tests)
       (optional, when non-zero);

"cached"?:<number> number of cached sub-goals verdicts (including Qed proved sub-goals)
       (optional, when non-zero).

    Notice that the JSON report file is printed in compact form without extra space nor indentation,
unless verbose level is greater than 2 or debug level is greater than 1.

### 2.8 Structure of Report Templates

Reports are created from user defined wp-report specification files. The general format of a wp-report
file is as follows:

<configuration section...>  chapter...>
@HEAD
<head contents...>
@CHAPTER
<per chapter contents...>
@SECTION
<per section contents of a
@TAIL
<tail contents...>
@END

The configuration section consists of optional commands, one per line, among:

@CONSOLE the report is printed on the standard output.
       Also prints all numbers right-aligned on 4 ASCII characters.

@FILE "<file>" the report is generated in file file.

@SUFFIX "<ext>" the report is generated in file base.ext,
       where base can be set with -wp-report-basename option.

@ZERO "<text>" text to be printed for 0-numbers. Default is "-".

@GLOBAL_SECTION "<text>" text to be printed for the chapter name about globals

@AXIOMATIC_SECTION "<text>" text to be printed for the chapter name about axiomatics

@FUNCTION_SECTION "<text>" text to be printed for the chapter name about functions

@AXIOMATIC_PREFIX "<text>" text to be printed before axiomatic names.           Default is
       "Axiomatic" (with a trailing space).

@FUNCTION_PREFIX "<text>" text to be printed before function names. Default is empty.

@GLOBAL_PREFIX "<text>" text to be printed before global property names.        Default is
       "(Global)" (with a trailing space).

@LEMMA_PREFIX "<text>" text to be printed before lemma names. Default is "Lemma" (with a
       trailing space).

@PROPERTY_PREFIX "<text>" text to be printed before other property names.

<!-- page 55 -->

    The generated report consists of several optional parts, corresponding to Head, Chapter and Tail
sections of the wp-report specification file. First, the head contents lines are produced. Then the chapters
and their sections are produced. Finally, the Tail content lines are printed.

    The different chapters are about globals, axiomatics and functions. Outputs for these chapters can
be specified using these directives:

@CHAPTER <chapter header...>

@GLOBAL <global section contents...>

@AXIOMATIC <per axiomatic section contents...>
       For each axiomatic, a specific section is produced under the chapter about axiomatics.

@FUNCTION <per function section contents...>
       For each function analyzed by WP, a specific section is produced under the chapter about functions.

@SECTION <default section contents...>

@PROPERTY <per property contents...>
       For each property of a section, a specific textual content can be specified.

    Textual contents use special formatters that will be replaced by actual statistic values when the
report is generated. There are several categories of formatters (PO stands for Proof Obligations):

Formatters        Description

&<col>:           insert spaces up to column col
&&                prints a "&"
%%                prints a "%"
%<stat>           statistics for section
%prop             percentage of proved properties in section
%prop:total       number of covered properties
%prop:valid       number of proved properties
%prop:failed      number of remaining unproved properties
%<prover>         PO discharged by prover
%<prover>:<stat>  statistics for prover in section

Provers     A prover name (see -wp-prover)
(<prover>)
            number of generated PO
Statistics  number of discharged PO
(<prover>)  number of non-discharged PO
total       maximal time used by prover for one PO
valid       maximal steps used by prover for one PO
failed      range of maximal steps used by prover (more stable)
time        percentage of discharged PO
steps
range
success

    Remarks: &ergo is a shortcut for &alt-ergo. Formatters can be written "%.." or "%{..}".
When range is used instead of steps, the maximal number n of steps is printed as a range a..b that
contains n. When option -wp-report-json is used, the previous rank a and b are kept when available
and still fits with the new maximal step number. Otherwise, a and b are re-adjusted following an
heuristics designed to increase the stability for non-regression testing.

    Textual contents can use naming formatters that will be replaced by current names:

<!-- page 56 -->

Names       Description

%chapter    current chapter name
%section    current section name
%global     current global name (under the chapter about globals)
%axiomatic  current axiomatic name (under the chapter about axiomatics)
%function   current function name (under the chapter about functions)
%name       current name defined by the context:
            - property name inside @PROPERTY contents,
            - function name inside @FUNCTION contents,
            - axiomatic name inside @AXIOMATIC contents,
            - global name inside @GLOBAL contents,
            - section name inside @SECTION contents,
            - chapter name inside @CHAPTER contents.
